Śilappaḍikāram
(‘the jewelled anklet’)
------------------------------------------
This is an epic poem in Tamil considered equal in literary quality to the Rāmāyaṇa of Kamban (12th century A. D.). Assigned to the 5th century A. D. it was composed by Iḷaṅkovaṭikaḷ. Nothing is known about him except that he was a prince of the country of Cera (comprising parts of the present Tamil Nadu and Kerala).
The epic poem describes the story of कण्णगि and her husband Kovilan. After living happily with his beautiful wife कण्णगि, Kovilan fell in love with a dancer Mādhavī and so deserted his legally wedded wife. After wasting all his wealth with the dancer, Kovilan returned to his wife कण्णगि who received him warmly.
Since they were very poor now, Kovilan took one of the two jewelled anklets of कण्णगि (which was their only possession now) to the market in the capital city of मदुरै, to sell. Meanwhile the queen of Neḍuñjeliyan (the king of Pāṇḍyan dynasty) had lost one of her anklets and the soldiers were searching for the thief. When they saw Kovilan trying to sell his anklet, they mistook him for the thief and killed him. When कण्णगि learnt of the tragedy she went to the king and accused him of murdering her husband. Out of shock, the king died on the spot!
Kaṇṇagi cursed the city of मदुरै which was now engulfed in fire and then killed herself.
The goddess Mīnākṣī of मदुरै, however, saved the city from total destruction.
Kaṇṇagi was deified and became the patron deity of the city of मदुरै.

Śilpaśāstra
(‘science of dexterous crafts and industries’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Vedic sacrificial religion clearly demonstrates how advanced the ancient Hindus were in pure sciences like mathematics as also applied sciences like the building of yāgaśālās (sacrificial sheds) and rathas (carts and chariots).
Apart from the वेदस्, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, it is interesting to note that any organised body of know-ledge is also called a Veda since Veda in general, means knowledge. One such Veda—considered rather as an उपवेद or subsidiary Veda—is the Sthāpatyaveda. It is the Veda concerned with the स्थपति (chief architect or master-builder).
Its other names, more commonly used, are: शिल्पशास्त्र, Śilpavidyā, Vāstu-śilpa and Vāstuvidyā.
Original Teachers
Hindu mythical tradition ascribes this science to eighteen teachers of whom विश्वकर्म and मय, the well-known architects of देवस् or gods and असुरस् or demons, stand out as supreme.
Some of the others mentioned are: भृगु, अत्रि, वसिष्ठ, नारद, ब्रह्मा, कुमार and बृहस्पति.
Basic Treatises and Literature
The treatises on this subject are legion. Only a few of them may be mentioned here: Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi, Aṁśubodhinī, Aṁśumadbhedāgama, Bṛhatsaṁhitā, Kāśyapaśilpa, Mānasāra, Mayamataśilpaśātra, Samarāṅgaṇasūtra-dhāra and Vāsturatnāvalī.
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (320 B. C.), some पुराणस् like the Agnipurāṇa, Matsyapurāṇa, Padmapurāṇa, and the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa also contain a lot of material on this subject.
Four Divisions
The शिल्पशास्त्र is a very vast body of science and technology, arts and crafts.
It is generally divided into four sections, each dealing with a different area of subject. They are: Dharā (earth); Harmya (buildings); Yāna (vehicles) and Paryaṅka (bedsteads).
These four may now be dealt with separately, but briefly.
Dharā
Dharā means the earth. This section deals with the testing of a soil in various ways to determine whether it is fit for building what is intended, such as a village or a town, with the necessary structures. Town-planning, surveying and marking are also included.
Several types of designs of towns and cities are mentioned.
Harmya
Harmya is the general name for a building. Several types of it are mentioned such as prāsāda (palace or temple), मण्डप (open hall), सभा (auditorium), शाला (stable or stall) and raṅga (pavilion) apart from private dwellings. Details of standard bricks and stones, mortars, and methods of arranging the bricks and stones are also given. It is interesting to note that the ancient architects knew how to prepare a strong and superior kind of cement called vajralepa.
Buildings with several storeys have also been described.
Palaces of several varieties too, depending upon the status of the king, are mentioned in detail.
Works on building construction frequently use four technical terms as applied to the builders—the engineers and the craftsmen—which may be cited here. They are: the स्थपति (the chief architect who is an expert in all aspects of construction); the sūtragrāhi (the surveyor who is an expert in the art of measuring); the vardhaki (the painter); and the तक्षक (the carpenter and the sculptor).
Yāna
Yāna stands for any mode of transport.
Various types of carts and carriages (śakaṭas), chariots (rathas) and palanquins (śibikās) have been mentioned in these treatises. Details of designs helpful in making them are also given.
Rathas are constructed for ceremonial or ordinary drives of इदोल्स्, ब्राह्मणस् or kings, as also for fighting purposes. They are therefore, of several varieties and shapes.
Paryaṅka
Though this word literally means a cot for sleeping, several types of furniture (like thrones and chairs), ornaments (like crowns, bangles and necklaces), and household articles are also included in this section.
Epilogue
The discovery of the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन् (2500 B. C.) which is now considered to be a later phase of the Vedic civilisation, has conclusively proved that the Hindus knew the science and art of town-planning very well. Gorgeous descriptions of the cities and the palaces of अयोध्या and लङ्का in the Rāmāyaṇa or of the royal mansion of the Pāṇḍavas at इन्द्रप्रस्थ in the Mahābhārata are pointers to the high degree of the advanced state of the contemporary society even after allowing for poetical exaggerations.
The construction of altars for वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् involving complicated designs based on the geometrical science is also a pointer to a highly evolved technology mastered by the Vedic आर्यन्स्.
From the frequent mention of missiles like the ब्रह्मास्त्र and the Vimānas or flying carrier vehicles—including the fantastic Puṣpakavimāna—in the पुराणस्, we can surmise that our ancient fore-fathers either had a high degree of civilisation or at least high ambitions which they considered as not impossible of achievement.
It should also be noted that quite a few of the आगमस् and the पुराणस् whose origins might be traced to the pre-Christian era, deal extensively with the sciences involving town-planning, architecture, construction of various types of buildings and other structures as also chariots and images.
From all these materials available, it may be concluded that शिल्पशास्त्र was a well-developed field of science and technology even from the earliest period of our history.
See also MŪRTIŚILPAŚĀSTRA and HINDŪ TEMPLES.
